group.title: First contact
group.blurb: Everything you need in the first two minutes of any Dutch conversation: greeting, name, where you are from, numbers, and spelling.

topics.title: Greetings and goodbyes
topics.summary: Which hello fits which hour, how to say goodbye without sounding final, and the four ways Dutch people ask how you are.

blocks.body: Dutch splits the day into three greetings, and each one is written as **one word**. The time-of-day greetings are a little more polite than `hoi`, so they are your safe default with strangers, shopkeepers and colleagues.

blocks.note: In speech people swallow the first syllable: 'morgen, 'middag, 'avond. You will also hear goeiemorgen, which is the same word said fast.

items.nl: Dag mevrouw, mag ik u iets vragen?
items.en: Hello madam, may I ask you something?

blocks.body: The workhorse pattern is `tot` plus a time expression. It literally means "until", so it always says **when you expect to meet again**. Pick the one that matches reality and you sound native immediately.

blocks.title: Add a wish
blocks.body: Dutch people almost always tack a wish onto the goodbye: `Fijne dag!` (have a nice day), `Fijn weekend!`, `Fijne avond!`, `Prettige dag verder!`. Answering `Jij ook!` (you too) is enough.

sections.heading: Meeting someone for the first time

items.note: only if you have met before

blocks.title: Zien is not ontmoeten
blocks.body: `ontmoeten` is meeting for the first time, `zien` is seeing someone again. Saying `Leuk je te zien` to a stranger sounds like you have forgotten them.

items.nl: Goed, dank je! En met jou?

items.note: polite way to say not great

blocks.title: Always bounce it back
blocks.body: Dutch small talk expects the return question: `En met jou?` or `En met u?`. Leaving it out reads as uninterested.

key_takeaways: Time-of-day greetings are single words: goedemorgen, goedemiddag, goedenavond.
tot + time says when you will meet again, so pick one that is true.
Answer how-are-you and then bounce it back with En met jou? or En met u?
Goedenacht is only for going to bed, never as an evening greeting.

exercises.prompt: It is 15:00 and you walk into a bakery. What do you say?
exercises.explain: Goedemiddag covers roughly 12:00 until 18:00.

exercises.prompt: You are leaving a class that meets again tomorrow. The most natural goodbye is:
exercises.explain: Tot morgen names exactly when you meet again. Tot ziens is polite but sounds like you may not return.

exercises.prompt: Complete the goodbye: you will see your colleague again in ten minutes.
exercises.explain: Tot zo is for within the hour. Tot straks (later today) also works.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks Hoe gaat het met je? Give the standard positive answer plus the return question.
exercises.explain: En met jou? is the object form after met. En met u? is the formal version.

exercises.prompt: Build the question: how are you (formal)?
exercises.explain: Question word first, then the verb, then the subject het, then the rest.

exercises.prompt: Which greeting is written as ONE word in Dutch?
exercises.explain: Goedemorgen, goedemiddag and goedenavond are all single words.

exercises.prompt: You are introduced to your neighbour for the first time. Which is wrong?
exercises.explain: Leuk je te zien means nice to see you again, so it does not fit a first meeting.

exercises.prompt: A friendly wish on a Friday afternoon as you leave the office.
exercises.explain: Fijn weekend! is the standard Friday goodbye. Note weekend is a het-word, so no -e on fijn.

topics.title: Introducing yourself and others
topics.summary: Three ways to give your name, the matching three questions, and how to present someone else to a group.

sections.heading: Three ways to give your name

blocks.note: All three are equally common. Match the answer to the question you were asked and the exchange sounds natural.

blocks.title: Watch the verb heten
blocks.body:
`heten` means "to be called". Its stem is `heet`, which already ends in **t**, so the jij and hij forms do not get a second t.
- ik heet
- jij heet (never heett)
- hij/zij heet
- wij/jullie/zij heten

items.nl: Hoi! Ik ben Esther. En jij? Wie ben jij?
items.en: Hi! I am Esther. And you? Who are you?

items.nl: Hallo! Mijn naam is Esther. Wat is jouw naam?
items.en: Hello! My name is Esther. What is your name?

items.nl: Hallo! Ik heet Esther. Hoe heet jij?
items.en: Hello! My name is Esther. What are you called?

items.nl: Mag ik me even voorstellen? Ik ben Abhinav Mudgal.
items.en: May I introduce myself? I am Abhinav Mudgal.

items.nl: Ik ben de nieuwe collega van de afdeling verkoop.
items.en: I am the new colleague from the sales department.

items.nl: Hoe is uw naam, als ik vragen mag?
items.en: What is your name, if I may ask?

blocks.title: voornaam and achternaam
blocks.body: `de voornaam` is the first name, `de achternaam` the surname. Many Dutch surnames carry a `tussenvoegsel` (van, de, van der, van den). When someone asks `Hoe spel je dat?`, spell the tussenvoegsel too.
Point with `Dit is ...`, then switch to `hij` or `zij` and keep going. This is exactly what you do when you present your conversation partner to a group.

items.nl: Dit is Esther. Zij komt uit Nederland en zij woont in Amsterdam.
items.en: This is Esther. She comes from the Netherlands and she lives in Amsterdam.

items.nl: Dit is James. Hij spreekt Engels en Spaans.
items.en: This is James. He speaks English and Spanish.

items.nl: Haar lievelingseten is pasta met pesto.
items.en: Her favourite food is pasta with pesto.

items.nl: Zijn naam is Hein en hij is 62 jaar.
items.en: His name is Hein and he is 62 years old.

blocks.title: zijn and haar switch with the person, not with you
blocks.body: `zijn` = his, `haar` = her. Learners often keep saying `zijn` for everybody. If you are talking about Esther, it is `haar naam`, `haar broer`, `haar werk`.

blocks.title: Ask these six and you can introduce anyone

key_takeaways: Ik heet / Mijn naam is / Ik ben are interchangeable, match them to the question asked.
heten has stem heet, so jij heet keeps a single t.
Present a third person with Dit is ..., then continue with hij or zij.
zijn = his, haar = her, and they follow the person you describe.

exercises.prompt: A: Hoe ___ je? B: Ik heet Esther.
exercises.explain: The stem heet already ends in t, so no extra t is added.

exercises.prompt: Which answer matches the question Wat is je naam?
exercises.explain: Question and answer mirror each other: naam question, naam answer.

exercises.prompt: Introduce your partner to the group: this is Esther, she comes from the Netherlands.
exercises.explain: Dit is + name, then a fresh sentence with the pronoun zij.

exercises.prompt: Talking about Esther: complete with the right possessive. ___ naam is Esther.
exercises.explain: Esther is female, so haar (her). Zijn would mean his.

exercises.prompt: Which form is spelled correctly?
exercises.explain: Stem + t, but a stem ending in t never doubles: jij heet.

exercises.prompt: The polite opener before giving your name in a meeting.
exercises.explain: Mag ik me even voorstellen? = May I introduce myself?

exercises.prompt: Build: what is your name (informal, with jouw)?
exercises.explain: Question word, verb, then the subject jouw naam.

topics.title: Personal details
topics.summary: Country, city, neighbourhood, address, birth date, phone number, age and job: the questions every form and every first conversation asks.

blocks.body:
Origin uses the verb `komen` with the preposition `uit`. Two questions ask for it:
- `Waar kom je vandaan?` The word `vandaan` splits off and lands at the end.
- `Uit welk land kom je?` Here the preposition sits at the front, glued to `welk land`.

items.nl: Ik kom uit Edinburgh, de hoofdstad van Schotland.
items.en: I come from Edinburgh, the capital of Scotland.
My country of birth is Germany.

blocks.title: Some countries carry de
blocks.body: Most country names take no article, but a handful do: `de Verenigde Staten`, `de Filipijnen`, `de Dominicaanse Republiek`. So it is `Ik kom uit de Verenigde Staten`, never `uit Verenigde Staten`.
Living somewhere uses `wonen` plus `in` for a city or country, and `op` for some street types. Dutch cities are cut into compass districts and locals name them constantly.

items.nl: Ik woon in Amsterdam-Noord, dichtbij het filmmuseum.
items.en: I live in Amsterdam North, close to the film museum.
Which neighbourhood do you live in?

items.nl: Ik woon vlakbij café De Ceuvel.
items.en: I live right near café De Ceuvel.

rows: Mijn e-mailadres is naam apenstaartje mail punt nl.

blocks.title: Three Dutch formatting habits
blocks.body:
1. The street comes first, the number after it: `Elandsgracht 70`.
2. Months are written in **lower case**: `15 augustus 1988`.
3. Phone numbers are read in pairs: `06 12 34 56 78` is nul-zes, twaalf, vierendertig, zesenvijftig, achtenzeventig. The `@` sign is `apenstaartje` (little monkey tail).

sections.heading: Age, time in the country, work

blocks.title: Age uses zijn, not hebben
blocks.body: Dutch says you **are** a number of years: `Ik ben 37 jaar.` or `Ik ben 37.` Never `ik heb 37 jaar`. The unit stays singular: `jaar`, not `jaren`.

items.nl: Hoe oud ben je? Ik ben 37 jaar.
items.en: How old are you? I am 37.

items.nl: Hoe lang woon je al in Nederland?
items.en: How long have you lived in the Netherlands?

items.nl: Ik woon hier al twee jaar.
items.en: I have lived here for two years.
items.note: Dutch uses the present tense plus al, where English uses have lived

items.en: What kind of work do you do?

blocks.title: No article with professions
blocks.body: After `zijn`, a job name drops the article: `Ik ben arts`, `Zij is ingenieur`, `Hij is student`. Adding `een` is not wrong when you also add an adjective: `Hij is een goede arts`.

key_takeaways: komen uit for origin, wonen in for where you live.
Waar kom je vandaan? sends vandaan to the end of the sentence.
Age takes zijn and the singular jaar: Ik ben 37 jaar.
Street before number, months in lower case, phone numbers read in pairs.
No een before a job title after zijn: Ik ben docent.

exercises.prompt: Complete: C: Uit welk ___ kom je? D: Ik kom uit Schotland.
exercises.explain: welk + het-word singular: het land, so welk land.

exercises.prompt: Build the question: where do you come from?
exercises.explain: vandaan splits off from waar and goes to the very end.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence gives your age correctly?
exercises.explain: Age takes zijn, and the unit stays singular: jaar.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says where you are from correctly?
options: Ik kom uit de Verenigde Staten.
Ik kom van de Verenigde Staten.
Ik kom in de Verenigde Staten.
exercises.explain: de Verenigde Staten is one of the few country names that keeps its article, and origin uses uit.

exercises.prompt: Give your address the Dutch way: street Elandsgracht, number 70.
exercises.explain: Street name first, house number after it.

exercises.prompt: Which birth date is written correctly in Dutch?
exercises.explain: Day, month, year, and Dutch months are lower case.

exercises.prompt: Say what you do for a living (teacher), with no article.
exercises.explain: Professions after zijn take no een: Ik ben docent.

exercises.prompt: Build: I have lived in the Netherlands for two years already.
exercises.explain: Dutch uses the present tense with al. Time (al twee jaar) comes before place (in Nederland).

topics.title: Numbers and counting
topics.summary: 0 to a million, the backwards teens, when to write a trema, and how to say years, prices and phone numbers.

blocks.note: 13 and 14 are dertien and veertien, not drietien or viertien. Learn those two as exceptions and the rest are regular.

blocks.title: een or één?
blocks.body: `een` (no accents) is the article "a/an". `één` with two accents is the number **one**, used when you need to stress it: `Ik heb maar één fiets.` In running text most people write `een` and let context decide.

Dutch says the **unit before the ten**, joined by `en`, all written as **one word**. So 21 is "one-and-twenty".
- 21 = `eenentwintig`
- 45 = `vijfenveertig`
- 78 = `achtenzeventig`
- 99 = `negenennegentig`

blocks.title: When to write a trema
blocks.body:
If the unit ends in a vowel that would clash with the `en`, Dutch writes a **trema** (the two dots) to show where the syllable breaks. That only happens with **twee** and **drie**.
- 22 = `tweeëntwintig`
- 23 = `drieëntwintig`
- 24 = `vierentwintig` (no clash, no trema)
- 53 = `drieënvijftig`

blocks.title: Listen to the end first
blocks.body: When a Dutch person says a phone number or price, the last part you hear is the ten. `vierenzestig` is 64, not 46. Train your ear by writing the second half of the word down first.

blocks.note: Dutch uses a dot for thousands and a comma for decimals: 1.250,50 is one thousand two hundred fifty euro and fifty cents.

items.note: read in pairs, so twaalf, vierendertig, zesenvijftig, achtenzeventig

blocks.body: Add `-de` up to 19 and `-ste` from 20 upwards. Four forms are irregular and worth memorising: `eerste`, `derde`, `achtste`, `veertigste`.

items.nl: Ons appartement is op de derde verdieping.
items.en: Our flat is on the third floor.

items.nl: Dit is mijn eerste les Nederlands.
items.en: This is my first Dutch lesson.

key_takeaways: 13 and 14 are dertien and veertien, 30 and 40 are dertig and veertig, 80 is tachtig.
From 21 up, the unit comes first and everything is one word: vijfenveertig.
Only twee and drie take a trema: tweeentwintig is written tweeëntwintig.
Ordinals take -de up to 19 and -ste from 20, with eerste, derde and achtste irregular.

exercises.prompt: Write 22 in words.
exercises.explain: Unit first, then en, then the ten. twee plus en needs a trema: tweeëntwintig.

exercises.prompt: Which number is vierenzestig?
exercises.explain: vier (4) plus en plus zestig (60) gives 64. The ten is always the second half of the word.

exercises.prompt: Which spelling is correct for 40?
exercises.explain: 40 is veertig, one of the irregular tens alongside dertig and tachtig.

exercises.prompt: Write 305 in words (one word).
exercises.explain: driehonderd plus vijf, written as a single word.

exercises.prompt: You are on the third floor. How do you say it?
exercises.explain: derde is the irregular ordinal for 3.

exercises.prompt: Write 78 in words.
exercises.explain: acht + en + zeventig, one word, no trema because acht ends in a consonant.

exercises.prompt: Which one means 'a bicycle' rather than 'one bicycle'?
exercises.explain: een without accents is the article. één with accents stresses the number one.

exercises.prompt: Write 93 in words.
exercises.explain: drie + en + negentig. drie ends in a vowel, so the trema appears: drieënnegentig.

topics.title: The alphabet and spelling out loud
topics.summary: Dutch letter names in four easy families, plus the phrases you need when someone asks you to spell your surname over the phone.

blocks.body: Do not learn 26 letter names one by one. Almost all of them fall into four groups that rhyme with each other.

rows: B, C, D, E, G, J, P, T, V, W
bee, cee, dee, ee, gee, jee, pee, tee, vee, wee
F, L, M, N, R, S
ef, el, em, en, er, es
I, O, U, Q, X, Y, Z
ie, oo, uu, kuu, ix, i-grec, zet
blocks.note: Group 4 is the only one you have to memorise item by item. Y is often called i-grec or Griekse ij.

blocks.title: G and J trip up English speakers
blocks.body: Dutch `G` is said "gee" (like the English word gay) and `J` is said "jee" (like yay). English speakers regularly swap them. `W` is "wee", not double-u.

`ij` is the Dutch **lange ij**, treated almost as one letter. In handwriting and in capitals both letters get capitalised: `IJsselmeer`, not `Ijsselmeer`. When spelling out loud you can say "lange ij" to distinguish it from the letter y ("i-grec").

items.nl: A: Wat is je achternaam? B: Te Riele. A: Hoe spel je dat?
items.en: A: What is your surname? B: Te Riele. A: How do you spell that?

items.nl: T, E, spatie, R, I, E, L, E.
items.en: T, E, space, R, I, E, L, E.

items.nl: Van der Berg, met een streepje? Nee, aan elkaar.
items.en: Van der Berg, with a hyphen? No, as one word.

blocks.title: The tussenvoegsel
blocks.body: Dutch surnames often carry a small linking word: `van`, `de`, `den`, `van der`, `ter`. It is called the `tussenvoegsel` and it is written in lower case inside a full name (`Esther te Riele`) but with a capital when the first name is left out (`mevrouw Te Riele`).

key_takeaways: Ten letters rhyme with -ee, three with -aa, six start with e-, and seven are odd ones out.
G is gee and J is jee, the opposite of what English speakers expect.
ij is the lange ij and capitalises both letters: IJmuiden.
Hoe spel je dat? and Kun je dat herhalen? get you through any phone call.

exercises.prompt: How is the letter G pronounced when you spell in Dutch?
exercises.explain: G belongs to the -ee family and is said gee, rhyming with the English word gay.

exercises.prompt: Which group do F, L, M, N, R and S belong to?
options: they start with an e sound
exercises.explain: ef, el, em, en, er, es all begin with a short e.

exercises.prompt: Ask someone how to spell what they just said (informal).
exercises.explain: spellen has stem spel. With je after the verb in a question, no -t is added.

exercises.prompt: Which spelling of the lake is correct?
exercises.explain: The ij counts as one letter, so both parts take the capital: IJsselmeer.

exercises.prompt: You did not catch the spelling. Ask for a repeat.
exercises.explain: Kun je dat herhalen? = Can you repeat that? The second verb stays in the base form at the end.

exercises.prompt: How do you say the letter Y when spelling?
exercises.explain: Y is i-grec (or Griekse ij). I is ie and J is jee.

topics.title: Sounds and spelling rules
topics.summary: Short versus long vowels, why wonen becomes woon but zitten becomes zit, and the rule that no Dutch word ends in v or z.

blocks.body: This is the single most useful sound contrast in Dutch. One vowel letter in a **closed** syllable (a syllable that ends in a consonant) is **short**. Two vowel letters make it **long**.

blocks.note: Say them as a pair out loud. The long one takes clearly more time, and the mouth stays tenser.

blocks.title: Rule 1: open syllables need only one vowel
blocks.body: In `wo-nen` the first syllable ends in a vowel, so it is open and the `o` is already long. Cut the ending off and the syllable closes, so you must **double the vowel** to keep it long: `wonen` gives `ik woon`. Same for `lezen` giving `ik lees` and `spelen` giving `ik speel`.

blocks.title: Rule 2: short vowels keep the double consonant
blocks.body: In `zit-ten` the first syllable is closed, so the `i` is short. Cut the ending off and one consonant is enough to keep it closed: `zitten` gives `ik zit`. Same for `bellen` giving `ik bel` and `stoppen` giving `ik stop`.

rows: long o, needs two letters when closed
long e, doubled, and z becomes s
short i, one t is enough
short e, one l is enough

sections.heading: No Dutch word ends in v or z

blocks.body: At the end of a word, `v` is written `f` and `z` is written `s`. The letter comes back as soon as an ending is added.

blocks.title: Final consonants go quiet too
blocks.body: Even where the letter stays, the sound hardens at the end of a word: `hond` sounds like "hont", `rood` like "root", `heb` like "hep". This is why `hij heeft` and `ik heb` feel so different.

rows: no English match, round your lips on eh
no English match, the hardest one
long vowel plus a quick y
long vowel plus a quick w
blocks.note: ij and ei sound identical. Which one to write is pure vocabulary, so learn each word with its spelling.

blocks.title: The unstressed e
blocks.body: In `de`, `het`, `-en` and `-er`, the `e` is a lazy uh sound, not a clear e. `lopen` in normal speech is closer to "lope" than "lo-pen", because the final n is often dropped.

sections.heading: The consonants that mark a foreign accent

rows: scrape it at the back of the throat
s plus that same scrape, two sounds
lips together, softer than English w
rolled at the front or scraped at the back, both fine

key_takeaways: One vowel in a closed syllable is short, two vowels make it long: bos versus boom.
Closing a syllable means doubling the vowel (wonen gives woon), keeping it short means one consonant (zitten gives zit).
Words never end in v or z: blijven gives blijf, reizen gives reis.
ij and ei sound the same, so their spelling has to be learned word by word.

exercises.prompt: Give the ik-form of maken.
exercises.explain: ma-ken has an open syllable with a long a, so closing it needs two letters: maak.

exercises.prompt: Give the ik-form of zitten.
exercises.explain: zit-ten has a short i, so one t keeps the syllable closed: zit.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct ik-form of reizen?
exercises.explain: No Dutch word ends in z, so it is written s: ik reis, wij reizen.

exercises.prompt: Which pair shows short versus long?
exercises.explain: kat has a short a, kaas has a long aa. The other pairs are both short or both long.

exercises.prompt: Give the plural of het huis.
exercises.explain: The s at the end of huis goes back to z once an ending is added: huizen.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about ij and ei is true?
options: they sound identical, only the spelling differs
ei is only used in names
ij is always at the end of a word
exercises.explain: They are pronounced the same. Which spelling a word takes is vocabulary, not a rule.

exercises.prompt: Give the ik-form of blijven.
exercises.explain: v at the end of a word is written f: ik blijf, wij blijven.
